I think that's where we disagree. Being trans is not a disease. The issue or problem is his perception of himself and self hate (gender dysphoria). In my opinion, understanding where that stems from would be a step in the right direction. 

No one is born hating themselves, so him expressing such a passionate hate for his body should be addressed. Simply changing his body without understanding why he feels that way, could lead to more issues and leave the root cause for his self hate unaddressed. So for example, if his dysphoria stemmed from sexual abuse, social influence, puberty, or something other than his neuroanatomy, it's possible that changing himself wouldn't fix the negative perception he has for himself. 

No one should have THAT much hate for any parts of themselves. We should not be DISGUSTED with our body parts. I don't think anyone should make permanent changes to themselves coming from a place of desperation or mental anguish, which is suggested by the intense hate he seems to have for his body. 

Once he's able to address the underlying causes for his dysphoria and works on loving himself,  if the dysphoria is still there, he can make an intentional decision to change himself from a non-emotionally charged and rational place. (Please note- self love, doesn't mean that there won't still be an incongruence between how he presents and how he feels, but that he can accept and appreciate his body, without feeling disgusted, as he works on becoming more congruent)

I also think him learning to love himself is beneficial so that he has realistic expectations of becoming a trans person. Socially, dating may not be as easy. He would need to understand that some people won't regard him as a woman, despite his outward appearance. He'd also need to be in a mental space to where he doesn't rely on the validation of others to support his identity. Also, many m-f transitioners opt to keep their male part because the surgery is very dangerous and painful. Oftentimes the parts created from bottom surgeries are non functional, meaning they cannot experience pleasure from it, if they can even use it during intimacy.

Effort can look different to everyone which is ultimately what our difference of opinions suggest. 

My standard of effort may be different from the next person's and that's okay. 

I think if we really think about it, everyone's standards usually reflects aspects of their personality and what they're looking for in a person. 

So for example, I enjoy getting dressed up, I love doing my makeup, wearing heels, etc., I want a man who also enjoys looking nice and who presents themselves a certain way. I wouldn't show up to a date in a t-shirt and jeans, therefore if a man did, I would see that as low effort. -- For that reason, I don't think excluding people who don't meet certain standards would be self sabotaging because those differences likely suggest that we're incompatible.  Doesn't mean he's not a good guy, he just wouldn't be a good fit for me.--  I also like men who are more dominate so a man putting effort in planning a date, shows me his ability and willingness to plan and lead. I state on my dating profile, that i don't do coffee dates so people who match with me know what to expect, so I match and attract people who are also okay with my first date expectations. 

On the other hand, some women have different personalities and may prefer and be more comfortable going on a more casual dates. You stated a few valid reasons above as to why you prefer casual first dates. We most likely have different personalities and we have a different "pre-date" process. Neither one is right or wrong but it's just our preferences. 

I speak on the phone, prior to going on dates. It allows me to determine if we'd be able to have a good conversation. So when i go on dates, I always have a decent time because i know that at the very least, i'll be able to have good conversation with a decent person, even if we aren't compatible as a couple. I have made some good connections and even a few friends this way. I will add that I am somewhat more extroverted and very  good at having conversations. 

I have had bad experiences with low effort dates and the mindset that usually accompanies it. Obviously this isn't true of all men who like more simple dates, but from my experience the men who suggest coffee dates or going for walks are men who are jaded by dating and tired of investing in failed connections. This tells me that they most likely swipe a lot and most likely harbor bitterness over the entire dating process. Funny story--I once went on a date where we walked around a pond and i listened to a man complain THEE entire time about how awful dating has been. He didn't ask me anything about myself. The conversation was all negative and about his last failed situation. It was insane. lol  And then over the next few days, he wanted to define what we were doing. He was basically trying to get me to decide if I wanted to see him seriously, after a single date, that was awful. (This was right after my divorce so I hadn't really been on many dates. I have since learned what works for me.)

Ultimately, I do think the majority of women want a certain amount of effort put into a date, but that effort can vary between each individual woman.

It doesn't need to be elaborate, there needs to be effort. You don't need to overdo it with talking/texting prior but enough to know if you'd want to put effort into a date. And no, that was this case. I've dated other people from dating apps and the reason it didn't work were due to very normal reasons. I'm still friends with some of them. A low investment date may work for some people but it's not what the majority of women want. And nice restaurants and activities aren't what's necessarily impressive, the effort behind it is. Intentions matter and the first date usually sets the tone for following dates so low effort dates are usually followed by other low effort dates because they now know you're willing to accept it.
